q: In fact, success preparedness has been so de-emphasized in recent years that teaching it has become a lost art.
As you can see, they’re very basic—representing the least that is required for success in a Zoom or Google Meet lesson. But they’re also crucial.
The point system represents the essential bones for each of these skills. They must be in place first if you hope to make video distance learning effective.
It’s important to mention that preparation points are not a reward. They’re an evaluation. As such, an easy way to manage them is to have every student start off with 5 points.

First of all, if you allow them to turn their video function off, then all hope is lost. Most of your class will follow suit, and even if they are in front of their screens—which is highly questionable—very little learning is going to take place.

t: Why You Shouldn’t Correct Student Work
q: One of the worst kept secrets in teaching is that students don’t pay any attention to returned work. They may glance at the grade—if you leave one—but then they’ll stuff it in their backpack to throw away later.
Because few students actually show it to them, most parents will never see day-to-day corrected work. Those that do, that even know it exists, are too busy to go over it with their child.

The purpose of independent work isn’t to learn in its strictest sense. It’s to practice. It’s to groove the memory. It’s to sharpen the skill and make it second nature so they can build on its base the next day.
This approach is not only easier on you, and a remarkable time-saver, but it also results in greater performance and higher grades for them.
Or, better yet, have your students do it themselves as a daily reminder that practice and repetition is the pathway to knowledge, skill, and, ultimately, success.

t: Why Rules Are More Important Than Consequences
q: Because there are no magic consequences. They don’t exist. There are best practices—which we’ve developed here at SCM—but virtually any configuration of consequences can work.
Taught in a certain way, rules make every act of misbehavior a choice students know full well they’re making.
Because when students view misbehavior as a choice, they take responsibility for it. They feel genuine remorse. They reflect on their mistakes and privately vow not to make them again.
You must consistently enforce your rules or they mean very little. Consistent doesn’t mean most of the time. It means all the time.
With both sticklers in play, your students will know that misbehavior is 100% their choice and own doing.
This is the real magic and secret to exceptional classroom management .

t: Why Allowing Students To Turn In Work Anytime Is A Bad Idea me-is-a-bad-idea/
q: There is a growing sentiment among educational leaders that students should be able to turn in work anytime without penalty, even weeks after the due date.
Mountains of research confirm what your instincts are probably already telling you: Deadlines improve motivation , produce greater effort, and result in better performance.
Seeing work pile up causes immense stress. It creates discouragement and hopelessness as the task becomes more daunting as time goes on.
The discipline needed to meet deadlines trains students in critical life and success skills like time-management, punctuality, responsibility , and integrity.
The powers that be are hiding a removal of standards by calling them standards . They’re also stating that deadlines are discriminatory against certain groups of students.
Note: Of course, if students have excused absences, connectivity issues, special circumstances, etc., then teachers should adjust deadlines accordingly.

t: The Evil Culture Of Online Teaching
q: It’s a culture, you see, of perfection, competition, and long hours toiling away at your desk.
It’s a culture that boxes you in and forces you to be someone you’re not and never wanted to be.
Your students don’t need you to compete with TicTok, video games, or their favorite YouTube channels (nor can you). They just need you to be YOU and share your passion for your subject.
But nothing is going to be as effective as you, standing in front of the camera with your wits, humor, and personality.
It is you, and only you, that can build influential, behavior-changing, intrinsically motivating rapport.
So I encourage you, when your colleagues are zigging, zag to your heart’s content.

t: Teacher-Student Relationships And The Law Of Reciprocity of-reciprocity/
q: It works no matter your age or personality, what grade level you teach, or whether your favorite color is blue or burlywood.
The Law of Reciprocity states that when someone is nice to you, you’ll naturally want to be nice to them right back. It’s a deep-seated psychological urge that is embedded into our DNA.
If ever you glare, lecture, or use sarcasm, it can be hard to work your way back into their good graces. Privately, they’ll knock you down a few pegs in their trust book.
But in the midst of a society that no longer views politeness as a virtue, your refusal to hold grudges, get revenge, or be anything other than kind to your students is a superpower.
Children have a finely tuned BS meter. They can tell if you’re being inauthentic or manipulative.
For when you give without expecting anything in return, which feels awesome, your students will bend over backwards to pay you back.

t: Should You Allow Students To Wear Pajamas During Zoom Lessons
q: Allowing pajamas communicates to students that they’re not really in school and that expectations during Covid are lax, if they exist at all.
The smallest foundational expectations, however—those that appear frivolous at first glance but mentally prepare students for learning—are in fact incredibly powerful in the message they send.

If you allow pajamas, then here come the stuffed animals. Here come the waffles and cereal and laying in bed. It’s a slippery slope that will never end unless you create a boundary that protects their learning.
Add pajamas and the distractions and lack of commitment they can cause and it becomes next to impossible to teach effectively.
When we challenge students, on the other hand, when we set foundational standards for them, when we send the message that through hard work they can excel, they become transformed.
PS – Allowing a “Pajama Day” once a month or so is fun and I wholeheartedly endorse the practice.

t: How To Thrive During The Upcoming Covid-19 School Year
q: Sharply defined boundaries in the form of a proven classroom management plan protect learning, ensure fairness, and make managing behavior so much easier .
With a plan that every student understands inside and out, the teacher will have to do far less talking .

The happiest, most successful teachers are obsessed with organization and maintaining a pin-neat classroom. The reason, backed by science , is because fewer distractions equal better focus, listening, and behavior.

Being at your best and most rested will be more important than ever before. Sleep, moderate exercise , leaving school at a decent hour . . . these things will give you the physical strength and mental heartiness to handle the inevitable frustrations and surprises to come.
You must get to a place above the fray and craziness, so you can be the rock your students are going to need.
I was going to rack my brain and make a thousand adjustments if I had to to bring peace and joy to my classroom.

t: How To Teach While Wearing A Mask
q: After all, students need to see your mouth and facial expressions to fully grasp your meaning.
In normal circumstances, most teachers talk way too much. They over-explain and digress off topic.
Even if you’re not prone to excessive talking, the less you speak while wearing a mask the better off you’ll be. Try cutting your talking by half or even two-thirds.
Instead of talking, model everything —at least until your students can perform the same repeatable actions all on their own.
The key is to show them in exacting detail what they need to do or know to succeed all on their own before turning them loose.
Talk less, model everything, and focus on independence. It was good teaching before the pandemic. Now, it’s essential.

t: How To Support Your Students’ Mental Health During Covid
q: Fear and social isolation are causing a spike in anxiety, depression, and suicide ideation.
Just knowing that they’re not alone can provide great comfort. The fact is, we’re all struggling to some degree. By simply acknowledging it, you can help a lot of students.
A powerful antidote to feelings of depression and anxiety is to have purpose . Because of Covid, purpose for many has been shredded into a million little pieces.

Every day tell your students that you’re there for them. Tell them that you care for them, that you have their back, and that you’ll do your best to help them through any struggle or obstacle they’re facing.
If a student reports to you that they feel like harming themselves or others, or if they appear in any danger, then immediately contact your principal, counselor, and psychologist.

Never go beyond the support boundaried by your level of training and certification. Never speak to a student alone without others in the room or exchange emails without cc’ing your principal or counselor.

t: How To Make Your Online Lessons Irresistible To Students e-to-students/
q: The potential long-term impact on these students is staggering—and not just academically.
Nothing I’ve ever done as a teacher has generated more response from students than when I tell a story.
No strategy in the world has the potential to build a more immediate and stronger connection with students than storytelling—and it’s a connection that can be made just as well over video.
Just be sure that you like the book—because if you don’t, it will show.
We have to give them a reason beyond just their academic progress to want to be part of the class .

t: How To Limit Your Students’ Screen Time
q: According to the American Heart Association, children ages 8-18 spend an average of more than 7 hours a day on their phones, playing video games, or watching TV.
This underscores the importance for us to do our part in limiting their screen time.
While online in particular, you must, must, must teach lessons that show students one thing they must be able to do or know.
Have them complete their work using good ol’ lead and timber—which has unique benefits that we’ll also cover in the future—while you observe from your end.
I recommend a ratio of 1:4—that is, your lesson to their independent work time. This way, you cut way down on their screen time while at the same time accelerating improvement.
Most critical, however, at least when it comes to their long-term health, it gets students offline.

t: How To Increase Student Online Participation By 50 Percent n-by-50-percent/
q: A few of which have been entirely off the grid for the past two months, whereabouts unknown.
Sorry, but if a family has internet access and the child is on TikTok and watching Netflix instead of doing their school work, then the parents aren’t doing their job.
Here at SCM, our team has had success getting more students involved and doing their work—up to 50% more—by speaking directly to the student.
It’s important that you don’t ask for assurances . You’re using your position as their teacher as leverage to get them moving, and thus you must tell them what they need to do.
Nearly every student we were able to talk to ended up turning in work within a day. And here’s the best part: They didn’t backslide.

In other words, give your students a chance to complete all previous assignments with no penalty. This is a tough time and many are just acquiring the self-starter skills they need to learn from home.

t: How To Handle The Uncertainty Of Next School Year
q: It’s understandable. There is so much we don’t know, so many hows, whys, and what ifs.
It does you no good to worry about things that may never come to pass. Furthermore, unless you’re in a position of leadership, it’s out of your hands.
One of the keys to avoiding stress is to not concern yourself with anything out of your control.
You see, with a strong classroom management plan, and the confidence in knowing that you can bring peace to your classroom no matter what comes your way, there is really nothing to worry about.
In 30 years of teaching, I’ve seen a zillion new procedures, policies, and protocols come down the pike and not one of them has managed to shake the foundations of good solid classroom management.
Enjoy your time off. Sleep in. Spend more time with family and good books (and bad TV). Have an adult beverage.

t: How To Handle Parent Complaints About Grades
q: Thus, it’s best to speak directly to the parent—if not in person, then over the phone. This way, you control the tone and spirit of your message, which is even more important than what you actually say.
Your first order of business is to just listen and grasp the crux of their complaint . You must get to the bottom of why they’re unhappy. Often, it’s different than you expect.
You must be able to share a percentage, score, unmet standard, rubric, inventory, key, or other objective measure. Always, always, always.
With the parent’s understanding of the grade, and what it takes to improve it, you’ll empower them to help and support their child. They’ll also leave the meeting with a greater appreciation of you.
It’s important to emphasize that a calm and friendly demeanor is the number one key to a successful meeting with parents. Any defensiveness or hostility from you will sabotage the process.

t: How To Handle Overbearing Teacher Colleagues
q: They dominate every meeting. They brag about and must share the way they do things and hardly listen to anyone else.

You must let go of any desire to be in charge and allow them to lead discussions and group meetings. By giving them what they want—to be heard and taken seriously—they tend to relax and temper their aggressiveness.
It’s important that you don’t bring up topics that get them off track. The best way to do this is to just be quiet. Speak as little as possible.
This is especially important: When it’s time to offer your opinion, do so directly, clearly, and with as few words as possible. Do not hem and haw or beat around the bush.

Once you’ve decided on a path that is in your control, don’t waver for anything in the world. Do not give in. As soon as you do, you’ll lose their respect and they’ll try to push you around even more.
The old adage to keep your friends close and your enemies closer is a truism based on this wisdom.

t: How To Give Your Students Hope
q: With students experiencing profound mental health struggles because of the pandemic, I’ve taken a different approach to teaching this year.
After all, Covid or not, children need purpose. They need direction and responsibility and a metaphorical kick in the pants.
Since the start of school, I’ve drenched my students in a downpouring of hope. In the midst of so much uncertainty, fear, and isolation, I believe it’s our primary duty as teachers.
I reorient them toward simple pleasures, those that must be savored, appreciated, and cultivated or else will die dry and withering upon the vine.
So I sit and I breathe. I close my eyes and prepare for class by thinking of them, my students, and what it must be like in their shoes—confused, lonely, life on hold.
It’s my job now to guide them through, to help them navigate the forest dark. To convince them that though we can’t see the light, it’s there.

t: How To Get Students To Turn On Their Zoom Camera
q: It’s to teach and behave in such a way that students want to turn their camera on.
When students see that perfect doesn’t exist, that even their teacher has interruptions and dogs barking in the background, then they’re more likely to join in.
The pressure to be perfect— the evil culture —has infected our profession with a dark seriousness that makes it drudgery.
You must loosen up all on your own and refuse to be a victim of circumstance or the whims of your school district.
It’s okay to smile and laugh and have fun with your students online, as it is in the classroom.
We use the power of reciprocity and belongingness to inspire students to make the right decisions on their own behalf.

t: How To Ensure Students Wear Masks And Socially Distance ocially-distance/
q: The likelihood, however, is that masks and social distancing will be the policy whenever you go back to school.

I think upon entering campus again for the first time—with its hand-washing stations, directional markings, plexiglass barriers, and regimented movements—students will realize the seriousness of what they’re about to undertake.
My recommendation then during the first week back to school is to just observe.
Keep your mask on and covering your nose and mouth at all times unless given permission to remove it.
Making it part of your classroom management plan is the only effective way to ensure masks are worn and social distancing is maintained.
Grab hold of your peace of mind and hang onto it for all it’s worth.

t: How To Ease The Strain On Your Students’ Mental Health
q: You see, when children have limited choices in their life, as they do now, they begin to lack a sense of their own value and worth—two areas that are being pummeled by social distancing mandates.

Choices, of course, must be given within the boundaries of your classroom management plan. You also have to be careful about giving too many, as this can cause them to freeze up and become indecisive.
With one-third of all Americans showing signs of clinical anxiety and depression, many previously and barely noticeable areas of our lives have now grown into critical importance.
Something taken for granted can explode into a necessity or in its absence become a strain on our mental health.
It can give students some personal power and control at a time when they have very little of either.

t: How To Cut Your Preparation Time And Lower Stress
q: In the late 1980s, an Italian software developer named Francesco Cirillo created a way to shorten work-related tasks while producing better results.
Set a timer for 25 minutes. This block of time is called a pomodoro.
Protect your pomodoros at all costs. Let nothing short of emergency interrupt you.
The Pomodoro Technique works because it creates a powerful sense of urgency that is both highly motivating and maximally efficient.
Parkinson’s Law is the tendency to expand a task in complexity in relation to the time given for its completion.
Over time, however, and what is so cool about it is that it actually trains you to become smarter, faster, and more focused.

t: How To Capture And Hold Your Students’ Attention On Zoom ntion-on-zoom/
q: You’re going to stand up during directed lessons. This one thing will cause you to teach more authentically and make your lessons worth watching.
It’s why top performing YouTubers rarely share their screen. They know that it’s them and their uniqueness that draws viewers and keeps them watching.
By moving a few feet away from your camera, students can see your body language and hand gestures.
Invite your students to stand and mimic your moves. Use hand gestures, body movements, and echoing to get students physically involved in their learning.

It’s hard enough for students to be separated from friends and social interaction. That they have to sit and stare at yet another screen and watch videos rather than receive real teaching is a tragedy.

t: How To Avoid Parent Complaints About Online Learning https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2020/05/09/avoid-parent-complaints-about-online-learning/
q: They can note every frustration, every moment of confusion, and every small struggle their child experiences. They can even sit right next to them during Zoom meetings .
The reason is because it’s an invitation to negotiate the amount or content of the work.
Any overly familiar language in your communiqués with parents and families can lower their perception of you as an authority.
Try never to leave room for interpretation. Avoid nuance at all cost and be direct and narrow in your definitions of what you expect.
Take the high road instead by being patient. Listen first. Breathe. Be gentle and understanding.
You must live it and breathe it with your high proficiency, internal strength, and bold, cold, hard truth.

t: An Easy Way To Build Rapport Online (Or In Class) https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2020/09/26/an-easy-way-to-build-rapport-online-or-in-class/
q: It’s to leave short, personal notes for individual students after class has ended.
Avoid trite language like “good-job” and “way-to-go,” which have lost their meaning due to overuse. Now they make students feel as if they’re just another face in the crowd.
Specificity is the key to finding the most influential words to put in your message. Focus on things your students would never in a million years think anyone would notice.
Kids these days are more aware than we think and can identify a phony from a mile away. So whatever you write in your note, make sure it’s honest.
In this way, you build your reputation as someone who can be trusted—which is crucial to having influential, behavior-changing relationships with even the most challenging students.
This generation, world-weary and jaded in so many ways even before Covid, shrug in the face of flattery and compliments that made students blush not ten years ago.

t: 5 Great Summer Books For Teachers
q: The reason is to keep my writing as authentic and untainted as possible. It must be based on what I see, what I experience, and what I have success using myself.
The Oxygen Advantage explains how to breathe in such a way that avoids the physical manifestations of stress, which in turn calms the mind and eliminates anxiety.
It also played sweet music into my disdain and rejection of extrinsic rewards .
Essentialism made me take a hard look at how I was spending my time and empowered me to double-down on what matters most in my life and has the greatest positive influence on others.
But this book makes the case through mountains of research into performance that the way a skill is practiced and learned makes a huge difference in success.

t: 10 Ways To Slow Down And Sleep Well After A Long Day Of Teaching
q: The good news is that you don’t have to put up with it. You don’t have to stand by and watch it happen to you. With a little discipline, releasing the pressure valve isn’t so hard.
The Navy SEALs famously use box breathing to calm themselves before and after missions. It clears the mind, slows the heart rate, and improves performance.
Walking has been shown to lessen feelings of anxiety, stress, and depression, increase self-confidence, and improve the quality of your sleep. It’s also a potent fat-burner.
This is one of the most powerful stress relieving strategies I’ve ever come across. And though incredibly simple, it works like magic.
The worst thing you can do is to prep for the next day of teaching in the evening. Better to be less prepared and energetic than over-prepared and in need of sleep.
The impediment to action advances action. What stands in the way becomes the way.

t: Things That Help: Weekly Wrap-Up Video for Parents
q: This isn't something I've done for my students' families but, gosh, does it seem like a simple method for radically increasing teacher clarity, teacher credibility, and the home-school partnership.
Ed's polish and poise is the fruit of hard-won expertise. He's been teaching English for 32 years and has coached 80 seasons (!) of football, wrestling, and lacrosse.

Mr. MC has made it easy to believe that their child is in the class of a credible teacher — someone who cares, is competent, and is passionate. Ed is nailing CCP, and when you do that with parents, you end up having parents reinforcing your credibility with their children.

This weekend, the parent/guardians of Mr. MC's students won't need to have vague conversations about what's happening in their English class — they'll be able to talk about sentence length, or home-writing, or what it means to be a better student.
Too often, the relationship between teachers and parents/guardians becomes borderline adversarial. I'm sure that Ed experiences this sometimes, but with messaging like this it's got to be rare.

Perhaps best of all, from a teacher workload perspective Ed hasn't created a monster here. He's taking lesson planning pieces that he already needs to create, and he's sharing them via screencast with parents.

t: How I Handled Misbehaviors on the First Day of Zoom Classroom
q: They were taking turns flashing their videos on and off, making funny faces each time they'd appear. I could tell they were getting a real kick out of it.
I told the student that we don't speak like that to one another, and then I removed him from the Zoom. This was the first day of Zoom class all year.

Hey, do you understand why I can't have you and Student X flashing your videos on and off like that? I'm not trying to pick on you guys, but I do want a place where we can all focus when we're on Zoom together.

I did not want to fall into the trap of placing any more time or effort into this one situation; after all, Student X is one of a hundred or so students on my rosters this semester, and I owe a shot at an education to all of them.

I remember thinking that day, "Well, I really hope Student X is in class tomorrow." I prayed that he would be. And I noted that Student Y volunteered his voice during our whole-class discussion twice.
First, I am working to like Student X — to genuinely value, know, and respect him. I want to like him no matter how he treats me.
A student's treatment of me (and you) is rarely personal, and even when it is, I don't need to take it to heart.

t: Things That Help: Lisa Van Gemert's Content Capsules Method or-creating-joyful-knowledge-rich-learning-spaces-remotely-or-in-persoon
q: In a nutshell, you choose critical vocabulary, explicitly teach it, review it often in ways students enjoy, use it regularly, and quiz it frequently.
The review activities do not need to be time consuming, but they need to be frequent. It's far better to have frequent, short review experiences than a single, extended experience.
In the 1880's, Herman Ebbinghaus conducted a series of experiments (on himself!) to test how quickly people forget learned information. He found that the rate of forgetting was shocking.

Ebbinghaus believed that every review experience meant you could space further review farther apart (so you need to review less and less frequently as you move on). You do, however, need to review close to initial instruction.
What most teachers do is teach something, assign a practice assignment, perhaps review that assignment, and then move on until there is a test. Then, they give a review of all of that learning.
With Concept Capsules, we review frequently, and we begin the review immediately.

To the brain, there is no such thing as "easy" or "hard." There is only "familiar" and "unfamiliar." By using the Concept Capsule method, I ensure to the greatest extent possible that my students enjoy a sense of ease so their abilities can shine through.

They must be introduced from a place of encouragement and even excitement. If your attitude is, "Well, here's one more thing they're expecting me to do," your students will feed off that attitude. It's contagious.

t: Things That Help: Emails as Letters
q: What if email didn't exist and all that we had instead was physical mail? Here's how my three sources of email would look in that scenario.
On default, it saturates and addicts. It's always open in a tab. So the second I get an urge to check it, I can.
It's also important to watch that I'm Only Handling It Once (OHIO). OHIO is life-giving — it honors the people who genuinely need to hear back from me (students, parents, colleagues, bosses).
All that we tend to accomplish with undisciplined work email checking is… Anxiety. Tension. Pressure. Like those things? Not me.
About three months into COVID, I realized, "Dude. I'm probably not going to travel any time too soon. Why is email on my phone?" Delete.
A while back I gave myself permission to unsubscribe from literally anything that I didn't like seeing in my inbox. Now I've got less than five email newsletter subscriptions — the rest are toast.

Now… they don't. Because now I know that each Friday afternoon, I get to sit down, C. S. Lewis style, at my writer's desk, and I get to correspond from the fullness of my humanity with other people in the fullness of their humanity.
It's the last working hour of my week, and I love it. So emails are letters.
